clue.text: Game to make one seasick?

definitions.meaning: a gambling game in which coins are pitched at a mark and then tossed
a ship that heaves up and down and rolls about will turn the stomach of a passenger

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading: the two verbs describe a boat's motion in rough water.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names an old coin-throwing game and also the two motions of a vessel that bring on nausea.

clue.text: Father has a sentimental song, but the youngsters swallow it

parts.note: pop is an informal word for a dad
corn is mawkish, sentimental material, as in a corny ballad

explanation.surface: Dad likes a soppy ballad, but the children just put up with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' looks like 'tolerate' in the surface; in fact it is literal: the snack is eaten by children.
explanation.definitionFit: A snack of puffed kernels is a favourite treat that children munch at the cinema.

clue.text: A short stroll round one Italian town

indicators.note: round says the stroll word goes around the letter for one

parts.note: a turn is a brief walk, as in taking a turn round the garden
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A brief walk around an Italian town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Piedmont city is a major settlement of northern Italy.

clue.text: In-flight cuisine?

parts.note: reads like airline meals, but means dining on a raised platform where college dons eat

explanation.walkthrough: 'In-flight' suggests aeroplanes; here a flight is a lofty position, as in the dais at the top of an Oxford or Cambridge college hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The raised dining board in a college hall is where fellows eat, literally an elevated meal.

clue.text: Standard opening reply when catechised

definitions.meaning: the Book of Common Prayer catechism begins 'What is your Name?', answered '....', meaning give your name

explanation.walkthrough: The Anglican catechism's first answer is printed as N or M, a blank for the child's own name; run together, those letters give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the expected benchmark, and the catechism's first printed response is spelt with those letters.

clue.text: Friar's on the ball, though kids may scoff at it

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: Friar Tuck is Robin Hood's companion; his possessive gives TUCK'S
a hop is an informal dance, so a ball

explanation.surface: A friar dances at a ball, though children may sneer at him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scoff' seems to mean mock; it means gobble food. A school shop selling sweets is a British institution.
explanation.definitionFit: British schools had a little shop selling snacks and sweets, which pupils eagerly devour there.

clue.text: Turn up jazz piece (American) — listen to the beat

indicators.note: in a down clue, turn up means the pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a rag is a piece of ragtime music

explanation.surface: Turn the volume up on a jazz number and hear the rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat' heard aloud is beet, the crop sweetener is extracted from; 'Turn up' turns RAGUS around.
explanation.definitionFit: Heard aloud, the phrase becomes beet, a root crop refined into sweetener for the table.

clue.text: How kitchen' boy gets up

parts.note: describes the lad who rotated a roasting rod over the fire in old kitchens, read as a phrase of how he rises

explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen boy's whole job named him: he rotated the roasting rod over the hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: Old kitchens employed a lad to rotate meat on a rod before the fire, and his title came from that task.

clue.text: State of Galilee troubled by, one's absence'

indicators.note: troubled tells us the letters of Galilee are stirred up into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The condition of Galilee was disturbed by someone being missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' rearranges GALILEE, and 'by one's absence' says the I (one) is left out of the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To state something is to assert or claim it, often without proof.

clue.text: Drug cargo ripe for disposal

indicators.note: goods for disposal are to be sorted and dealt with, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A shipment of ripe drugs is ready to be got rid of.
explanation.definitionFit: An old opium-and-camphor remedy for coughs and diarrhoea is a medicinal preparation.

clue.text: Thin food for semi-giant

indicators.note: semi means half, so only the latter half of the giant's name is kept

parts.note: Pantagruel is the giant in Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel

explanation.surface: Watery fare served to someone of only half-giant size.
explanation.walkthrough: The giant is Rabelais's Pantagruel; 'semi' drops its first half, PANTA.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin porridge of oats boiled in water is watery fare, famously given to Oliver Twist.

clue.text: Elaborate a point — talk around it

indicators.note: talk around it says the speech word encloses the point

parts.note: to orate is to talk pompously or make a speech
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Develop a point at length by speaking around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elaborate' looks like a verb; it is the adjective meaning fancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something richly decorated and intricate is fancy and detailed.

clue.text: Turn away from Latin — it is one summit after another

parts.note: est is Latin for it is
a range of mountains is a line of peaks one after another

explanation.surface: Abandon Latin, which is one peak after another to climb.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to drive them off or make them cool towards you.

clue.text: Order given to, say, Ben Battle

indicators.note: an order given to some words puts their letters into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A command issued to someone called Ben Battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ben Battle' looks like a man's name; the battle is the 1645 Civil War defeat of Charles I in Northamptonshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1645 English Civil War engagement where Cromwell's New Model Army defeated the king was a famous fight.

clue.text: In Erasmus, detailed translation from ancient tongue

indicators.note: a translation turns words into another form, so these letters are rearranged
detailed means having the tail cut off, so the final letter goes

explanation.surface: Erasmus produced a detailed translation from an old language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' drops the last letter of ERASMUS to give ERASMU, and 'translation' rearranges IN plus ERASMU.
explanation.definitionFit: The language of ancient Mesopotamia's first cities is one of the oldest written languages.

clue.text: A slip on the mountain pass causes a fall

indicators.note: on means the slip is added after the pass in this across answer

parts.note: a col is a pass between two peaks
a lapse is a slip or error

explanation.surface: Losing your footing on an Alpine pass leads to a tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden caving in or tumble down is a fall.

clue.text: King dressing up finds' new courage

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the dressing word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: oil is a salad dressing
heart means courage, as in take heart

explanation.surface: A monarch putting on his robes discovers fresh bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressing' looks like putting on clothes; it is salad oil, turned by 'up' to LIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard I of England was known by this epithet for his bravery as a crusader monarch.

clue.text: Hold back holiday — bad weather

parts.note: a rest is a break or holiday
rain is bad weather

explanation.surface: Bad weather keeps a holiday in check.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrain is to curb or keep someone or something in check.

clue.text: Appears to suppress, for example, dogfights

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held and printed as 'Appears to suppress, for example, dogfights (8)': the parse COMES around PET (dog, for example) with 'fights' as definition needs 'dog' and 'fights' as separate words, but they are printed as one word 'dogfights'.
annotationWithheld.clue: Appears to suppress, for example, dogfights

clue.text: Empty space in the Bible printed in Geneva, for example

indicators.note: printed in says the Bible's letters are set inside the place word

parts.note: Geneva is an example of a city
AV is the Authorised Version of the Bible

explanation.surface: A gap in the Bible version that was printed in Geneva.
explanation.walkthrough: The Geneva Bible is a real 1560 translation, which makes 'Geneva' look like part of the book's name rather than an example of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: A hollow is a void or hole inside something solid.

clue.text: Knows one is listening to a siren

definitions.meaning: heard aloud, knows is nose, and slang for a nose is the answer
a horn or whistle that sounds a warning

explanation.walkthrough: The first half works by sound: 'knows' heard is nose, and the answer is British slang for a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud warning horn is called this, and it is also British slang for a big nose.

clue.text: Find telephone' rent — it would be distressing if one were cut off!

definitions.text: it would be distressing if one were cut off!

parts.note: to ring is to telephone
to let is to rent out

explanation.surface: Find the phone bill; losing the line would be upsetting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distressing' splits as dis-tressing: cutting off a curl removes a tress.
explanation.definitionFit: A curl of hair is a tress, so snipping one off is literally dis-tressing.

clue.text: Account it extremely circumstantial truth

indicators.note: circum means around, so circumstantial says one piece stands around the others

parts.note: very means extremely

explanation.surface: An account that is highly detailed has the ring of truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circumstantial' looks like a description of evidence; split as circum-stantial, standing around, it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Veracity is truthfulness or accuracy.

clue.text: Leave chopped eel

indicators.note: chopped means the end of the fish's name is cut off

parts.note: a conger is a large sea eel

explanation.surface: Leave behind an eel that has been cut up.
explanation.definitionFit: A congé is a dismissal or permission to depart, as in French leave.

clue.text: Feature introducing work of composer

indicators.note: introducing means the work goes inside the feature

parts.note: the chin is a feature of the face
OP, opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: An article that introduces a composer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature' looks like a newspaper article; it is a facial feature.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polish-born pianist wrote nocturnes and polonaises and is a famous Romantic music writer.

clue.text: Lawmen have a hot drink — not, tea, we hear

indicators.note: not says the drink loses the letter that follows

parts.note: a posset is a hot drink of milk curdled with wine or ale

indicators.note: we hear says tea is the sound of a letter of the alphabet

parts.note: tea, said aloud, is the letter T

explanation.surface: Sheriff's men take a warm drink, but apparently not tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A posse is a band of men summoned by a sheriff to keep order.

clue.text: Weapon' to exercise in midweek

indicators.note: in places the exercise inside the middle letters

parts.note: the middle two letters of the word week are E and E
PE is physical education, exercise

explanation.surface: A sword used for fencing practice in the middle of the week.
explanation.definitionFit: A fencing sword with a stiff blade is a duelling weapon.

clue.text: Writer Kipling never expected to meet

definitions.meaning: Mark ..., the author of Huckleberry Finn
Kipling wrote 'East is East, and West is West

explanation.walkthrough: The second half alludes to Kipling's Ballad of East and West, where the two are said never to meet.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain is an American author, and in Kipling's line the word means the pair of East and West.

clue.text: Valuing a friend, fill him with .. endless encouragement

indicators.note: fill him with means the friend is packed with the next piece

parts.note: a pal is a friend

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is removed

parts.note: praise is encouragement

explanation.surface: Weighing up a mate, you should give him boundless praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'him' refers back to the friend, so 'fill him with' tells you what goes inside the friend; 'endless' trims the final letter of the encouragement word.
explanation.definitionFit: An appraisal is an assessment of worth, so it is the act of estimating value.

clue.text: Again laying out check garment

parts.note: to rein is to check or curb
a vestment is a robe or garment

explanation.surface: Laying out the clothes again and checking a robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laying out' looks like arranging clothes; it means spending money.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting money into an investment a second time is spending it again.
